the Moving Party on this Motion

Robby Bernstein
and
Archie J. Rabinowitz
,
Counsel for Ronald C. Rutman, Estate Trustee during Litigation of the Estate
of Paul Penna, one of the Respondents on the Motion

Fred Tayar
, Counsel for a number of the Charities
who are the Applicants in this proceeding and Respondents on the Motion

Justin de Vries
, Counsel for Langston, one of the
former Estate Trustees of the Estate of Paul Penna, and a Respondent on the
Motion

Michael W. Kerr
, Counsel for Ernie Sheriff, one of
the former Estate Trustees of the Estate of Paul Penna, a Respondent on the
Motion and taking a watching brief only on the Motion

HEARD:
JANUARY 22, 2007

REASONS:
GREER J.

[
1
]

The late
Paul Penna (“the deceased”) died on August 29, 1996, leaving his widow,
Lorraine Penna (“Lorraine”) surviving him.  Lorraine had a life interest in her
late husband’s estate and on her death, the residuary beneficiaries were a
number of charities, most of whom are the Applicants in the proceedings before
the Court.  Lorraine and Charles Langston (“Langston”) and Barry Landen
(“Landen”) were the Estate Trustees named in the deceased’s Will.  They
administered the Estate until the death of Lorraine on December 18, 2003.
Although Lorraine Penna was removed as a Director of Jakmin Investments Limited
(a holding company as an asset in the deceased’s Estate), since she was said to
be incapable in 1999, it was not until her death, that Lorraine Penna was
replaced by Ernie Sheriff (“Sheriff”) and he became a co-trustee of the Estate with
Langston and Landen.  Sheriff had, however, replaced her earlier as a Director
of Jakmin.  What should have taken place on the death of Lorraine was a Passing
of Accounts of the Estate of Paul Penna to the date of her death.  That did not
happen and there is no evidence that the charities, which were the residuary
beneficiaries of the Estate, were ever informed of Lorraine’s death so they
could request such a Passing of Accounts.

[
2
]

At the
date of his death, the deceased left an estate having a value of approximately
$24,000,000.  As of February 2004 the Estate had only approximately $590,000
left in it.  The three original Estate Trustees chose not to probate the Will
and Landen, for all practical purposes, controlled and administered the Estate
both before and after the Lorraine’s death.  Eventually, Landen’s two
co-trustees retained LECG Canada Limited to do a forensic audit of the Estate
Accounts.  No accurate and complete Estate Accounts were ever kept by the
Estate Trustees.  The Estate Trustees were then removed by my Court Order in
2005 and Ronald C. Rutman (“Rutman”) became the Estate Trustee during
Litigation.

[
3
]

Under
Lorraine’s Will, she named her sister, Sylvia Bennett (“Bennett’’) and Landen
as her Estate Trustees.  Bennett brings this Motion on her own accord, with
Landen neither consenting nor opposing it, having chosen to take no part in it,
although all Estate Trustees, at law or as otherwise provided under the Will,
must act in unison.  I am satisfied, however, that Bennett had no choice but to
act alone in this matter, given Landen’s role in the Estate of the deceased.
The Motion has come about due to the estate litigation presently before the
Court, to which the Estate of Lorraine Penna is now a Respondent.

Relief requested under the Motion

[
4
]

Bennett
moves for the following relief:

(a)

for a Declaration that the Partial Summary Judgment Motion brought on by
Rutman, as Estate Trustee during Litigation, as well as any future claims for
damages brought against the Estate of Lorraine Penna, or its executors, arising
out of any alleged breach of legal duty by Lorraine Penna while acting as an
executor of the Estate of Paul Penna, are statute-barred;

(b)

for a Declaration that subparagraph (a) above be a defence to any and
all subsequent claims for damages brought against the Estate of Lorraine Penna,
or its executors, arising out of any alleged breach of legal duty by Lorraine
Penna while acting as an executor of the Estate of Paul Penna, in these or
related proceedings;

(c)

for an Order fixing the costs of this Motion on a substantial indemnity
basis, plus GST.

The Partial Summary Judgment Motion referred to above, was
served on Bennett and others, on December 4, 2006, seeking damages in the sum
of $412,353, jointly and severally, against Bennett and others.  The claim
against Bennett and Landen arises from an alleged breach of fiduciary duty
committed by Lorraine and Landen while they acted as Estate Trustees (formerly
Executors) of the Estate of Paul Penna.

[
5
]

It is the
position of Bennett that the two-year limitation period under the new
Limitations
Act 2002,

S.O. 2002, c.24
applies to the Partial Summary Judgment Motion
and to any other future claims for damages which may arise against the Estate
of Lorraine Penna, or its Estate Trustees, arising out of any alleged breach of
legal duty by Lorraine while acting as an estate trustee until her death on
December 18, 2003.  Bennett says that the expiry date for any claims to have
been made against Lorraine’s Estate is December 18, 2005, two years after her
death.  In taking this position, Bennett relies on provisions of the said
Limitations
Act 2002,
the
Trustee Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c.T.23, the
Estates Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c.E.21, and the
Courts of Justice Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c.C.43.

[
6
]

It is the
position of all Respondents taking part in the Motion, that the Motion must be
dismissed on the grounds that the two-year limitation does not apply in the
circumstances of this case, that Notice of the pending litigation was given to
the Estate of Lorraine Penna prior to the Partial Summary Judgment Motion
having been brought on, and that other aspects of the case must be taken into
account when the Court determines whether the limitation applies or not.

The Technicalities

[
7
]

The Estate
of Lorraine Penna moved with some haste to try to set this Motion down to be
heard on April 7, 2006.  I refused, as the Case Management Judge of the Paul
Penna Estate, to hear it at that time, as I found that the Motion was
premature, given that Lorraine’s Estate had not yet been sued by the
Applicants.  I then, on July 7, 2006, ordered that the Estate of Lorraine
Penna, be added as a party , given that I had, upon my removal of the Estate
Trustees, ordered a Passing of Accounts of the Estate of Paul Penna.

[
8
]

While
Bennett may not have been as fully apprised of these matters as Landen was, it
is clear that by the time the forensic accounting was begun by LECG in 2005,
Landen knew that the other Estate Trustees of Paul Penna’s Estate, namely
Langston and Sheriff, would be looking for the estate assets, many of which
were either missing or had been diverted from the Estate to other persons or
entities, who were not residuary beneficiaries of the Estate.  Fraud was being
alleged in connection with these missing or diverted assets.  Landen was
Bennett’s co-trustee and may have informed her of the possibility of such an
action being launched.  Since Bennett swore no Affidavit on this Motion (the
only Affidavit being that of counsel’s associate), there is no way of knowing
just what her knowledge was after Lorraine’s death.

[
9
]

The Estate
of Lorraine Penna took part in certain proceedings before the Court prior to
being served with the Partial Summary Judgment Motion, and discussions had
taken place among the various counsel involved in these proceedings.  The
involvement of the Estate of Lorraine Penna in these proceedings therefore came
as no surprise to her Estate Trustees.  Since they had never moved to Pass
their Accounts for the administration of her Estate before the alleged fraud or
alleged defalcation was discovered in her late husband’s Estate, these Estate
Trustees remained in place when this litigation began.

[
10
]

Langston, Sheriff and Jakmin
Investments Limited (an asset of the Paul Penna Estate) began their action
against Landen, his wife and their numbered company on March 1, 2005 by
Statement of Claim dated March 31, 2005.  The Estate of Lorraine Penna is not
listed as one of the Defendants.  On April 20, 2005, there was a meeting of
counsel for the original Applicants of the Estate of Paul Penna where it was
suggested by counsel for some of the charities, that a Claim may be brought
against the Estate of Lorraine Penna.

[
11
]

Bennett concedes that her counsel
was put on notice on May 13, 2005 of such a Claim, when counsel for some of the
charities wrote to the solicitor for Lorraine’s estate stating that she had
been advised of the Claim at the informal meeting on April 20, 2005, and that
she had, “…previously been put on notice that the beneficiaries of the estate
intend to look to Lorraine Penna’s estate for damages arising from her
negligence while she acted as an executrix of the Penna estate.”

[
12
]

Counsel for Bennett says one must
look at
S.47
of the
Estates Act

when examining notification of a claim
by a person against the estate of a deceased person.  It reads as follows:

(1)

The
Trustee Act

does not affect the claim of a person against the
estate of a deceased person where Notice of the claim giving full particulars
of the claim verified by affidavit, is filed with the executor or administrator
of the estate at any time prior to the date upon which the claim would be
barred by the
Trustee Act
, but where no executor or administrator has
been appointed, the Notice may be filed in the Office of the local registrar of
the Ontario Court (General Division) [now the Superior Court of Justice].

(2)

Where the claim of a person against any other person would be barred by
the
Trustee Act
at any time within three months after the death of the
person having the claim, the claim shall for all purposes be deemed not to be
barred until three months after the date of such death.

Therefore, if an ordinary creditor of Lorraine’s Estate
had a claim against her, which fell within this provision, and no executor or
administrator (now estate trustee) had been appointed, there would be an
extension of three months after her death to make the claim, if it would
otherwise be barred under the
Trustee Act
.

[
13
]

The claim against Lorraine, in
these proceedings, is not such a claim.  See: S.44 of the said Act.  It is a
claim arising out of her fiduciary role as one of the estate trustees of her
late husband’s estate.  There was both oral and written notice to Lorraine’s
estate that a Claim would be forthcoming as early as March 31, 2005, when
Lorraine’s co-trustee Langston and the replacement co-trustee, Sheriff, took steps
against Lorraine’s other co-trustee, Landen.  Clearly, by April 20, 2005, when
the informal meeting of various counsel took place, Lorraine’s estate was on
notice that the claim against her in her capacity as an estate trustee, would
be brought.

[
14
]

Formal Notice of the Partial
Summary Judgment now issued was served on Bennett as one of Lorraine’s Estate
Trustees, on December 4, 2006, seeking damages against Lorraine’s Estate.
Bennett was aware that the Applicants intended to do so, claiming that such damages
arose out of her alleged breach of a legal duty by her while acting as an
estate trustee of her late husband’s estate.

The
Trustee Act
and the former
Limitations
Act

[
15
]

Prior to the enactment and the
coming into force of the
Limitations Act
2002, when such claims were
made, one looked to the provisions of the former
Limitations Act
, the
Estates
Act

and the
Trustee Act
and to the case law to see how limitations,
if any, applied.  Under subsections 38(2) and (3) of the
Trustee Act
,
actions against executors and administrators for torts were brought as follows:

(2)

Except
in cases of libel and slander, if a deceased person committed or is by law
liable for a wrong to another in respect of his or her person or to another
person’s property, the person wronged may maintain an action against the
executor or administrator of the person who committed or is by law liable for
the wrong.

(3)

An
action under this section shall not be brought after the expiration of two
years from the death of the deceased.

Under the provisions of the then
Limitations
Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c.L 15, S.43(2)
, dealing with actions against trustees,
states:

In an action against a trustee or a person claiming
through a trustee, except where the claim is founded upon a fraud or fraudulent
breach of trust to which the trustee was party or privy, or is to recover trust
property or the proceeds thereof, still retained by the trustee, or previously
received by the trustee and converted to the trustee’s use, the following
paragraphs apply:

1.  All rights and privileges
conferred by any statute of limitations shall be enjoyed in the like manner and
to the like extent as they would have been enjoyed in such action if the
trustee or person claiming through the trustee had not been a trustee or person
claiming through a trustee.

S.44(2) of that Act then goes on
to state, where there is a claim of a beneficiary against a trustee:

44(2)  Subject to section 43, no claim of the beneficiary
of a trust against the trustee for any property held on an express trust, or in
respect of any breach of such trust, shall be held to be barred by a statute of
limitations.

It can be thus
seen, that the Legislature, in enacting these provisions, intended to exempt
claims for fraud or fraudulent breach of trust or conversion of trust property,
from all limitation provisions.  See:
Edwards v. Law Society of Upper
Canada
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14677 (ON CTGD)
, 39 O.R. (3d) 10, [1998] O.J. No. 963, Court File NO.
94-CQ-48311 (O.C.J. (Gen. Div.)) at p.6, Quicklaw.  That decision of Mr.
Justice Sharpe, as he then was, was upheld by the Court of Appeal at (2000)
2000 CanLII 4122 (ON CA)
, 48
O.R. (3d) 321, [2000] O.J. No. 2084 Docket Nos. C29476 and C29477.  See: para.
13 of the Quicklaw version.  This case has been followed by Mr. Justice Howden
in his recent decision,
Cameron (Estate) v. Button,

[2005] O.J. No. 1671

Newmarket Court File No. 69234/03 (S.C.J.).

[
16
]

Counsel for Langston points out
that under these previous rules, one could also look to the discoverability
rule, a judge-made rule of statutory interpretation.  In
Re Canadian Red
Cross Society
,
(2002) 62 O.R. (3d) 277 (S.C.J.)
, Regional Senior Justice
Blair, as he then was, notes that this judge-made rule allows a limitation
period to be extended to that date when where all the material facts on which a
claim is to be made have been discovered by the plaintiff or ought reasonably
to have been discovered through the exercise of reasonable diligence.  He also
analyzes, in that case, how “special circumstances” can apply to give the judge
discretion in extending a limitation period.

[
17
]

Master Dash also, in
Eade
(Litigation Guardian of) v. Browne Estate

(2005), 15 E.T. R. (3d) 304, 21
M.V.R. (5
th
) 288 (S.C.J.)
, analyzes when “special circumstances”
might apply to add a party to a proceeding after the limitation period has
expired.  Counsel for Langston says that this discretion has not disappeared
under the new
Limitations Act 2002
, and that it should be considered by
me, if I find that this new Act protects the Estate of Lorraine Penna from a
claim being made against it.

The
Limitations Act 2002
,
S.O. 2002, c.24

[
18
]

The new
Limitations Act

2002

was proclaimed in force on January 1, 2004.  It is the position of Bennett
that this is the legislation that applies and that any claim the Estate of Paul
Penna may have had against Lorraine, or now against her Estate, is barred,
since the two-year limitation would have begun on Lorraine Penna’s death on
December 18, 2003 and expired on December 18, 2005.  Bennett’s position is that
only proceedings based on equitable claims by aboriginal peoples against the
Crown are now exempt from the two-year limitation and that no other persons
with equitable claims are exempt.  S.2(1) of the Act sets out other exemptions
but estate proceedings or claims for fraudulent breach of trust are not listed.

[
19
]

Bennett then relies on S.19(1) of
the Act, which states that a limitation period set out in or under another Act
that applies to a claim to which this Act applies is of no effect unless the
provision establishing it is listed in the Schedule attached to the Act.  The
Schedule referred to therein does list
subsections 44(2)
and
45(2)
and
47
of
the
Estates Act
and
S.38(2)
of the
Trustee Act
.

Bennett’s
position is that the two-year limitation therefore applies since S.38(2) causes
the Partial Summary Judgment Motion to be statue-barred.

[
20
]

Bennett points to
Driedger on
the Construction of Statutes
, 3
rd
ed. by Ruth Sullivan,
Butterworths, Toronto, P.279, where the author states that materials set out in
a schedule may be given the force of law by being incorporated into the Act to
which they are appended.  Generally, says Driedger, the incorporation is
obvious and explicit.  Even if such Schedule is not incorporated, says
Driedger, it may be relied on in interpreting the Act.

[
21
]

While the above may be the case,
the Respondents say that the Transition Rules, as set out in S.24 of the new
Limitations
Act
govern the current circumstances.  It defines “former limitation
period” as a limitation period that applied in respect of the claim before the
coming into force of this Act.  S.24(2) reads:

(2) This section applies to claims based on acts or
omissions that took place before the effective date and in respect of which no
proceeding has been commenced before the effective date.

[
22
]

It is clear that the act or
omission in question took place before January 1, 2004 and that no proceeding
had been commenced before January 1, 2004.  It is the position of the
Respondents that even if the claim was to be based on an act of omission that
took place after January 1, 2004, the
Limitations Act, 2002
would not
apply.  They say that there is therefore no limitation period, which can apply
to the claim that the Estate of Paul Penna may have against the Estate of
Lorraine Penna and her Estate Trustees.  The alleged acts or omissions took
place some time between the date of death of Paul Penna and when the Claim was
made by Langston, Sheriff and Jakmin against the Landens.

[
23
]

Section 24(2) of the Transition
Rules states that this section applies to claims based on acts or omissions
that took place before the effective date, January 1, 2004, and in respect of
which no proceedings has been commenced before the effective date.  In
Hare
v. Hare
,
2006 CanLII 41650 (ON CA)
, [2006] O.J. No. 4955, Docket: C45293 (O.C.A.), a case involving a
demand loan, the majority of the Court found in paragraph 48, that the act of
delivery of the Note took place in February 1997 and so pursuant to s.5(2) of
the new
Act
, the appellant was presumed to have “discovered” her claim
in February 1997, that is, before January 1, 2004.  The Court found that Rule 2
of s.24(5) therefore applied, so that the former limitation period applied.

[
24
]

In the case at bar, there was no
formal limitation period which applied under previous legislation.  Although
the Schedule to the new
Act
includes
S.38(2)
of the
Trustee Act
,
it did not apply in the case at bar, because S.44(2) of the then
Limitations
Act
, took such claims out of any limitations period.

[
25
]

S.24(6) of the Transition Rules
applies where there was no former limitation period.  It reads:

(6) If there was no former limitation period and if
a limitation period under this Act would apply were the claim based on an act
or omission that took place on or after the effective date, the following rules
apply:

1.

If the claim was not discovered before the effective date, this Act
applies as if the act or omission had taken place on the effective date.

2.

If the claim was discovered before the effective date, there is no
limitation period.

Rutman says, Section 24(6), by its express terms can
only apply if two conditions are met, namely there was no limitation period
before January 1, 2004, and a limitation period under the new
Limitations
Act
would apply if the claim was based on an act or omission that took
place after January 1, 2004.

[
26
]

Rutman says, if the answer is
“yes”, then Rule 1 or Rule 2 under Section 24(6) applies.  If the answer,
however, is “no” and there was no limitation period before the effective date,
then there continues to be no limitation period after the coming into force of
the new
Limitations Act
and Rules 1 and 2 under s.24(6) do not even get
considered.

[
27
]

Since a limitation period under
the new Act would not apply if the claim was based on an act or omission that
took place on or after the effective date, because the limitation period under

s.38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
would apply if the claim was based on an act
or omission that took place on or after the effective date.  However, a
limitation period under another Act, that is S.38(3) of the
Trustee Act
,
is not, by definition, a limitation period under the new
Limitations Act
.
Therefore, the answer to the question as to whether a limitation period under
the new Act would apply if the claim was based on an act or omission that took
place after the effective date is “no”.  Therefore the second condition under
S.24(6) is not satisfied.  Since only the first condition is satisfied under
s.24(6), there continues to be no limitation period applicable to the action.
See:  the LAWPRO Transitional Rules Table (a copy filed in the Respondent
Rutman’s brief of authorities) and Graeme Mew's Transitional Rules Table (same
as LAWPRO’s) –
The Law of Limitations
, Second Edition, page 20 and
Ontario
Limitations Manual’s Transitional Rules
Table – 3rd ed., Appendix-2.

[
28
]

The Notice of Action was issued on
March 1, 2005, the Statement of Claim in the Action was issued on March 31,
2005 and Bennett and Landen were not added as Parties to the Action in their
capacity as the Estate Trustees of the Estate of Lorraine Penna until July 10,
2006, when they became parties to the Order to Pass the Accounts of the Paul
Penna Estate.  The Partial Summary Judgment Motion not served on Bennett until
December 4, 2006, which was after the “effective date” under the
Act
.
Therefore, there continues to be no limitation period applicable to the claim
made by Rutman.

[
29
]

Counsel for the Respondent
charities raises the point that neither the old nor the new Act precludes a
claim for equitable fraud.  It is not necessary to analyze this point, as I
have found, as noted above that there is no limitation period, which applies
under these circumstances, given the wording of the Transition Rules.  If I had
not found so, in my view, the discoverability rule would still apply under the
circumstances of this case, and the Estate of Lorraine Penna would properly be
a party.

[
30
]

I am, however, of the view, that
Rutman’s alleged claims are for fraud, against Landen and perhaps others.  The
allegation is that Landen knew exactly what was taking place when monies were
removed from the Estate of Paul Penna.  In cases of fraud, as opposed to
equitable fraud, the person so alleging that fraud has taken place, is claiming
that the dishonest acts were deliberately committed, not that they arose out of
an honest mistake.  When fraud is found, any such claim for damages results in
a damages award not being subject to any bankruptcy proceeding, which may be
launched by the fraudster at a later date.  Damages based on fraud survive
bankruptcy.  Damages arising out of an honest mistake do not.

[
31
]

Rutman also alleges breach of
fiduciary duty on the part of all the former Estate Trustees.  The charities
also point out that Bennett cannot escape having a claim made against her, even
if Landen did not respond to it in his position as a co-trustee.  I agree with
that proposition.

Conclusion

[
32
]

Given the above analysis, there is
no limitation period, which prevents Rutman from adding Bennett and Landen, in
their capacities as Estate Trustees of the Estate of Lorraine Penna, as parties
to this action, for purposes of the claim now made against them.  Bennett’s
Motion is therefore dismissed in its entirety.  Order to go accordingly.

[
33
]

If the parties cannot otherwise
agree on Costs, I will receive brief Written Submissions from counsel regarding
the same, with the Respondents filing their brief, together with time dockets
and a Bill of Costs, with me within 30 days of this Order, with Bennett to
reply within 10 days thereafter.  If the Respondents require any Reply to
Bennett’s submissions, they shall have 10 days after its receipt to so Reply.
Orders to go accordingly.

___________________________

Greer J.
